kernel: A ghost story that is funny and frightening in equal measure. You inherit a decrepit canal boat with a resident ghost who insists he is still the captain and will not let the boat leave its mooring. Your only living companion is your brother-in-law, who came to help you sell it and who wants his money back more than he wants you safe. I want the ghost to be a real character, scary when he needs to be, and I want the boat to actually go somewhere.

shape.note: through_lines is how many distinct story lines (each with its own ending) the shape preference suggests; the review decides whether each next one is worth building.

protagonist.who: You are the new inheritor of a narrow canal boat, standing on its stern deck with your brother-in-law already counting the cost of every rope, lock, and drop of fuel.
protagonist.wants: to get the boat under way and sold without losing your brother-in-law's nerve or your own authority over the vessel
protagonist.can_do: inspect the boat, untie and retie the mooring line, take the helm, sign or refuse the sale papers, pay or refuse to pay the lock fees, and answer the ghost directly
protagonist.cannot_do: make the boat leave its mooring or enter a lock without first satisfying whatever condition the ghost has placed on the water, the wheel, or the sale, because the ropes, timbers, and gates answer to his captaincy before they answer to you

arena.description: The inherited narrowboat itself, moored at a canal lock, with its stern deck, cabin, and wheelhouse as the only places you can stand while the lock gates wait at the boat's stern.

pressure.description: The sale is being pushed toward completion as dawn approaches, and your brother-in-law insists the boat must be shown moving before any buyer will pay.
pressure.clock_or_stock: none tracked; the urgency is told through the approaching dawn and the buyer's arrival, but neither is a losing outcome

opposition.who_or_what: your brother-in-law, who came to help sell the boat and has turned the haunting into a column in his ledger
opposition.wants: his money back and the boat sold before the ghost makes the sale impossible or the boat too frightening to buy
opposition.means: he holds the sale papers, the cash for fuel and lock fees, and the key to the mooring chain, and he can sign the boat away to a buyer who will not wait, withhold payment for the passage, or make every delay cost more

events.what: The mooring line snaps in the dark, not by wind but by the ghost's hand, and the boat drifts toward the lock while your brother-in-law screams at the price of the fuel it will take to hold it.

At midnight the ghost stands at the helm in full rigging and points out a crack in the hull that is only visible in the dark, while your brother-in-law tries to sleep in the cabin and hears the water move.
The boat refuses to enter the lock because the ghost demands a proper salute to the water, and the lock gates jam against the hull until the salute is made or the boat is turned away.

mediation.question: Does the boat move by the dead captain's terms, or by the living owner's hand?

to_reach_pole_a.what_you_must_do: let the ghost stand at the helm, answer his orders, perform the salute to the water, and let him name the course while your brother-in-law pays for the fuel and lock fees
to_reach_pole_a.cost: your brother-in-law's money and patience are spent, he is frightened and haggles the sale price down, and the boat moves under the dead captain's name, leaving you with a vessel that is no longer fully yours

to_reach_pole_b.what_you_must_do: sign the sale papers, pay the towpath keeper or lock keeper, cut or re-tie the mooring line, and force the boat past the lock by living means, such as turning it into the side cut or letting it be sold as a boat rather than a captain's vessel
to_reach_pole_b.cost: the boat's timbers groan, leak, or refuse, the ghost's displeasure makes the passage frightening, and your brother-in-law demands more money or signs the sale under worse terms

complications.description: The towpath keeper on the bank has seen the boat move before and says the water only answers to a salute, not to a sale.
Your brother-in-law's ledger already lists the ghost as a depreciation, and he is willing to sign the sale papers to the buyer before dawn if the price is high enough.

cast_seeds.wants: to recoup his investment in the sale before the haunting makes the boat unsellable
cast_seeds.holds: the sale papers, the cash for fuel and lock fees, and the key to the mooring chain
cast_seeds.edge: treats the ghost as a line item to be audited rather than a presence to be feared
cast_seeds.tie: is your brother-in-law and came to help you sell the boat, but his loyalty is to his ledger more than to you
cast_seeds.voice: speaks in financial terms even when terrified: 'If the ghost wants a salute, does it come with a receipt? I need to know if this is a deductible expense.'
cast_seeds.breaking_point: signs the boat away to the first buyer who won't wait if the water level drops again without a clear cost-benefit analysis
cast_seeds.name: Lazlo Brandt

cast_seeds.wants: to maintain command of the vessel according to his old, rigid nautical code
cast_seeds.holds: authority over the boat's timbers, the wheel, and the water's response to the hull
cast_seeds.edge: is terrified of being forgotten but insists on being obeyed, even when his orders cause the boat to leak
cast_seeds.tie: was the boat's captain before you inherited it, and views your inheritance as a usurpation of his post
cast_seeds.voice: speaks in archaic, formal nautical commands with zero humor: 'The water is not ready. You are not ready. Stand by.'
cast_seeds.breaking_point: turns the boat against the lock gates if you attempt to cut the mooring line without first performing the salute
cast_seeds.name: Lake Kaur

cast_seeds.wants: to keep the lock operational and avoid liability for a boat that refuses to move
cast_seeds.holds: the control of the lock gates and the physical ability to jam or release them
cast_seeds.edge: has seen too many strange things on the canal to be surprised by a ghost, but is annoyed by the paperwork
cast_seeds.tie: is paid to manage the waterway, and your brother-in-law's delays cost him overtime he didn't budget for
cast_seeds.voice: talks in bureaucratic complaints: 'If the boat won't move, I can't fill the chamber. If I can't fill the chamber, I can't clock out. This is a scheduling issue.'
cast_seeds.breaking_point: refuses to work the lock if the ghost makes the water look wrong, and makes you answer for the delay
cast_seeds.name: Pell Szeto

cast_seeds.wants: to maintain the towpath and collect the proper salute from passing vessels
cast_seeds.holds: the right to demand a salute to the water and the knowledge of which boats are 'cleared' to pass
cast_seeds.edge: is superstitious about the canal's moods and will not let a boat pass if the water looks 'wrong'
cast_seeds.tie: is the only person who remembers the old rules of the canal, and your brother-in-law's impatience is an insult to tradition
cast_seeds.voice: speaks in riddles and warnings: 'The water remembers. Does it remember you? No. Then you must make it remember.'
cast_seeds.breaking_point: blocks the towpath if you fail to perform the salute, regardless of your brother-in-law's cash
cast_seeds.name: Stellan Ilunga

framework.name: Three-act structure
framework.shape: a want is disturbed, pursued through complications that reverse at the midpoint and bottom out in a crisis, then settled in one decisive confrontation

modifier.name: Episodic middle
modifier.effect: Each middle beat is a self-contained instance of the story's recurring decision with its own small ending; what carries across them is what the protagonist is becoming.

framework.reading: The story begins with the boat stuck and the living owner's authority compromised, building through escalating, specific negotiations with the ghost as the sale deadline approaches. It should land on a decisive moment where the boat finally moves, resolving the tension between the dead captain's terms and the living owner's agency in a way that is both frightening and funny.
framework.why: The story follows a sustained trajectory of complications (the recurring instances of the ghost's conditions) that reverse at the midpoint (the midnight discovery) and bottom out in a crisis (the jammed lock gates) before settling in the decisive confrontation of the boat moving, which matches the 'want is disturbed... settled in one decisive confrontation' shape.

beats.name: Setup
beats.job: the protagonist's situation and want before the disturbance, shown through something they do

beats.name: Inciting incident
beats.job: the disturbance that makes the want urgent and the old way of getting by impossible

beats.name: Commitment
beats.job: the protagonist commits to one way of pursuing the want; from here there is no going back to the setup

beats.name: Midpoint
beats.job: a reversal or revelation that changes what the pursuit means or what it will cost

beats.name: Crisis
beats.job: the low point: the chosen way fails or its price comes due, and the opposition has the upper hand

beats.name: Climax
beats.job: the decisive confrontation, where the story's question is answered by what the protagonist does

beats.name: Resolution
beats.job: the new state of things: what the answer cost and what it left

T1.title: The Salute at Dawn
T1.motivation: You start out wanting to prove you can command the boat and sell it before dawn, rather than be ruled by a dead man. By the end you want the boat to move under the captain it already has, even if that means your name is no longer the only one on it.
T1.strategy: Meet each of the ghost's nautical demands with a concrete living payment: answer his orders, pay with Lazlo's cash, and give his ledger a receipt for every fright.
T1.turning_point: At midnight, the ghost points to the dark crack and Lazlo prices the fear. You realize the boat cannot be sold as a dead man's vessel unless you first let him name what is wrong with it.

ending.title: Under the Dead Captain's Name
ending.summary: The boat moves because you let Lake Kaur stand at the helm and name the course, while Lazlo pays for the fuel, the lock fee, and the lowered sale price. It has cost you full authority over the vessel and left you with a boat that is no longer entirely yours.
lost: the sale papers as originally written
ending.changed: the boat is sold under the dead captain's name and moves to the lock with a crack in the hull that only shows in the dark

T2.title: The Chain Mark
T2.motivation: When the line snaps, you come to want to stop the boat by something you can hold and pay for, because Lazlo Brandt hands you the key to the mooring chain and prices the scrape before you can answer the ghost. By the end you want the boat sold and moving under your own signed authority, even if that means the dead captain is no longer aboard.
T2.strategy: Take the chain, keep the boat under your own hand, let Lazlo Brandt carry the buyer's mark and the cash, and get the boat sold and moving before the water can be saluted.
T2.turning_point: The mooring chain key. Once you hold the key and Lazlo Brandt prices the scrape as a buyer's mark, the boat stops being something to answer the ghost and becomes something to sell under your own name.
T2.differs_from: T1 answers with the dead captain's authority and loses only the mooring line and the original sale papers; this line answers with the living owner's agency and loses Lake Kaur, leaving the boat sold under your name with the chain mark still on the stern.

ending.title: The Chain Mark
ending.summary: The boat goes through the lock on your signature and Lazlo Brandt's fee, with the chain scrape still blackening the stern and the buyer paying less for the mark. Lake Kaur is left at the mooring, and the sale papers name you, not the dead captain.
ending.changed: the boat is sold under the living owner's hand and the dead captain is no longer aboard

divergence.trigger: you threw the spare mooring line to the lock chain
divergence.instead_of: you took the helm and answered Lake Kaur's order to bring the boat stern-first to the lock
divergence.opportunity: Lazlo Brandt hands you the key to the mooring chain and prices the scrape the chain will make before you can answer the ghost.
divergence.shift: The boat stops by the chain, not by the wheel, and Lazlo Brandt has already turned the scrape into a buyer's mark. From that moment you want to finish the passage by living payment and signature rather than by the ghost's salute.

T2.why: The seed holds as given: way 2 at N02 gives the line a physical, payable object—the mooring chain—and a mark the buyer will price. That lets the story answer the central question by pole_b: the boat moves under the living owner's signature and fee, and Lake Kaur is left behind instead of kept as captain.

T3.title: The Number for the Ghost
T3.motivation: Once Lazlo has priced the crack as a depreciation, you come to want a number for the ghost more than you want to be afraid of him, because his ledger gives you a way to keep the sale alive without saluting the water; by the end you want the boat sold and moving under a price the dead captain can no longer name, even if that price costs you Lazlo.
T3.strategy: Let the ledger set the ghost's cost, let Lazlo Brandt sign the boat away on his own terms, and take the boat into the side cut with Stellan Ilunga's bank rope.
T3.turning_point: The ledger's number. When Lazlo writes the ghost's depreciation into the sale papers, the haunting becomes a sum, and you stop answering the ghost and start answering the column.
T3.differs_from: T1 lets Lake Kaur stand at the helm and name the course, keeping Lazlo standing and paying with the lowered sale price; this line answers mixed by letting the ledger set the ghost's price and the bank rope move the boat, losing Lazlo to the sale he priced and leaving the ghost's shadow aboard. T2 gets the boat through under your signature and leaves Lake Kaur at the mooring; this line keeps the ghost's shadow aboard and makes the boat move by Stellan's rope and Lazlo's ledger, with Lazlo lost rather than standing.

ending.title: The Bank Rope
ending.summary: The boat is pulled into the side cut by Stellan's rope while the timbers groan and Lake Kaur's shadow stands in the porthole. Lazlo signs the boat away at the ledger's inflated figure, more than the buyer pays, and leaves with the buyer's lower cash. The sale is done without your name on the helm, and the boat is sold as a living ledger's vessel with the ghost's shadow still aboard.
lost: the sale papers as originally written
ending.changed: the boat is sold by the living ledger and pulled by the bank rope, with the ghost's shadow still aboard; Lazlo is gone with the buyer's cash, and the sale papers carry the ledger's number rather than the dead captain's course

divergence.trigger: you took the crack's price from Lazlo's ledger before asking the ghost
divergence.instead_of: you stood at the helm and let Lake Kaur name the defect
divergence.shift: Lazlo's ledger gives the crack a number before the ghost names it, and the number makes the ghost payable rather than salutable. You learn that the haunting can be written as a depreciation, and you come to want the number more than you want to be afraid of the man who made it.

T3.why: The seed holds as given: taking the crack's price from Lazlo's ledger before asking the ghost changes the haunting from a salute to be performed into a number to be paid, and the side-cut bank rope gives the boat a living means of movement that keeps Lake Kaur's shadow aboard without giving him the named course. The seed's ending world holds: the boat is sold by the living ledger and pulled by Stellan's rope, while Lazlo is lost to the sale he priced.

T3N02.title: The Side Cut
T3N02.summary: The boat refuses the lock and the gates jam against the hull because Lake Kaur demands a proper salute to the water. You cut the mooring line and hand the end to Stellan Ilunga, who pulls the boat into the side cut with the bank rope while Lake Kaur's shadow stands in the porthole and the timbers groan. Lazlo Brandt signs the final sale at the ledger's inflated figure, more than the buyer will pay, and hands the buyer's lower cash to Pell Szeto for the lock fee, saying the difference is a depreciation loss.

T3N03.adapted: The boat lies in the side cut with the sale papers signed at the ledger's number, and Lake Kaur's shadow remains in the porthole as the water settles. Lazlo Brandt walks down the towpath with the buyer's lower cash and his ledger, leaving the boat behind; the sale is done without your name on the helm, and the vessel moves as a living ledger's sale with the dead captain's shadow still aboard.

C01.label: your brother-in-law
C01.wants: to recoup his investment in the sale before the haunting makes the boat unsellable
C01.holds: the sale papers, the cash for fuel and lock fees, and the key to the mooring chain
C01.edge: treats the ghost as a line item to be audited rather than a presence to be feared
C01.tie: is your brother-in-law and came to help you sell the boat, but his loyalty is to his ledger more than to you
C01.voice: speaks in financial terms even when terrified: 'If the ghost wants a salute, does it come with a receipt? I need to know if this is a deductible expense.'
C01.breaking_point: signs the boat away to the first buyer who won't wait if the water level drops again without a clear cost-benefit analysis
C01.name: Lazlo Brandt

C02.label: the ghost captain
C02.wants: to maintain command of the vessel according to his old, rigid nautical code
C02.holds: authority over the boat's timbers, the wheel, and the water's response to the hull
C02.edge: is terrified of being forgotten but insists on being obeyed, even when his orders cause the boat to leak
C02.tie: was the boat's captain before you inherited it, and views your inheritance as a usurpation of his post
C02.voice: speaks in archaic, formal nautical commands with zero humor: 'The water is not ready. You are not ready. Stand by.'
C02.breaking_point: turns the boat against the lock gates if you attempt to cut the mooring line without first performing the salute
C02.name: Lake Kaur

C03.label: the lock keeper
C03.wants: to keep the lock operational and avoid liability for a boat that refuses to move
C03.holds: the control of the lock gates and the physical ability to jam or release them
C03.edge: has seen too many strange things on the canal to be surprised by a ghost, but is annoyed by the paperwork
C03.tie: is paid to manage the waterway, and your brother-in-law's delays cost him overtime he didn't budget for
C03.voice: talks in bureaucratic complaints: 'If the boat won't move, I can't fill the chamber. If I can't fill the chamber, I can't clock out. This is a scheduling issue.'
C03.breaking_point: refuses to work the lock if the ghost makes the water look wrong, and makes you answer for the delay
C03.name: Pell Szeto

C04.label: the towpath keeper
C04.wants: to maintain the towpath and collect the proper salute from passing vessels
C04.holds: the right to demand a salute to the water and the knowledge of which boats are 'cleared' to pass
C04.edge: is superstitious about the canal's moods and will not let a boat pass if the water looks 'wrong'
C04.tie: is the only person who remembers the old rules of the canal, and your brother-in-law's impatience is an insult to tradition
C04.voice: speaks in riddles and warnings: 'The water remembers. Does it remember you? No. Then you must make it remember.'
C04.breaking_point: blocks the towpath if you fail to perform the salute, regardless of your brother-in-law's cash
C04.name: Stellan Ilunga

L01.why: where the mooring line, sale talk, and lock fees are handled

L02.name: the wheelhouse

L03.name: the cabin
L03.kind: the enclosed living space inside the boat
L03.why: where Lazlo tries to sleep and hears the water move

plan.assessment: T1 answers the question for the dead captain: the boat moves only when Lake Kaur is allowed to stand at the helm and name the course, and the price is your full authority over the vessel. The missing worlds are the boat moving by a living hand without the salute, and a pole_a ending where a living companion is lost instead of only the line and the original papers. The story can part earliest at N02, when the snapped line can be answered by chain, ledger, or ghost-order rather than by the main line's answered helm.

seeds.motivation: When the line snaps and the boat drifts, you come to want to stop it by something you can hold and pay for, because Lazlo hands you the key to the mooring chain and prices the scrape before you can answer the ghost.
seeds.strategy: Take the chain, keep the boat under your own hand, let Lazlo carry the buyer's mark and the cash, and get the boat sold and moving before the water can be saluted.
seeds.trigger: you threw the spare mooring line to the lock chain

ending.title: The Chain Mark
ending.summary: The boat goes through the lock on your signature and Lazlo's fee, with the chain scrape still blackening the stern and the buyer paying less for the mark. Lake Kaur is left at the mooring, and the sale papers name you, not the dead captain.
ending.changed: the boat is sold under the living owner's hand and the dead captain is no longer aboard

seeds.why_different: T1 keeps the ghost as captain and loses only the original papers; this line loses the ghost and keeps the boat moving by your own signed authority, so the answer to the story's question is reversed.

seeds.motivation: Once Lazlo has priced the crack as a depreciation, you come to want a number for the ghost more than you want to be afraid of him, because his ledger gives you a way to keep the sale alive without saluting the water.
seeds.strategy: Let the ledger set the ghost's cost, let Lazlo sign the boat away on his own terms, and take the boat into the side cut with the towpath keeper's bank rope.
seeds.trigger: you took the crack's price from Lazlo's ledger before asking the ghost

ending.title: The Bank Rope
ending.summary: The boat is pulled into the side cut by Stellan's rope while the timbers groan and Lake Kaur's shadow stands in the porthole. Lazlo signs the boat away for more money than the buyer pays, and the sale is done without your name on the helm.
lost: the sale papers as originally written
ending.changed: the boat is sold by the living ledger and pulled by the bank rope, with the ghost's shadow still aboard

seeds.why_different: T1 keeps Lazlo standing and gives the ghost full command; this line loses Lazlo to his own sale note and makes the boat move by a mixed hand of ledger, rope, and ghost-shadow rather than by the dead captain's named course.

promises.reading: The reader wants a gothic comedy where the horror is bureaucratic and the comedy is domestic: a haunted vessel that refuses to move because its dead captain has a point, and a living heir who is too broke and too pressured to argue back. They want to feel the creak of the timbers and the sting of a sibling's impatience, balanced by the relief of a joke that lands right when the hair on the back of the neck stands up.
promises.player_fantasy: To be the reluctant captain of a haunted vessel, using wit and stubbornness to negotiate passage with a dead man while keeping a living man from selling the ship out from under you.

promises.what: a ghost who is terrifying in the dark but petty and specific in the light, enforcing nautical rules that no longer exist
promises.why: the Kernel demands a 'real character' who is both scary and funny; the humor comes from the ghost's rigid adherence to protocol, the fright from his power over the boat

promises.what: a brother-in-law who measures every creak in pounds and pence, treating the haunting as a depreciation issue rather than a supernatural one
promises.why: the Kernel specifies he wants his money back more than your safety; this provides the constant, grounded pressure that contrasts with the ghost's ethereal authority

promises.what: the boat itself as a responsive entity, groaning, leaking, or refusing to unmoor when the captain's conditions are not met
promises.why: the Kernel says the boat 'insists' it won't leave; the setting must feel alive and obstructive, not just a backdrop

promises.what: a sequence of escalating tests where the player must satisfy the ghost's 'captaincy' requirements to unlock movement
promises.why: the brief identifies the decision axis as labeling how to get the boat underway; the audience expects a puzzle of appeasement or defiance rather than a simple fight

promises.what: moments of genuine, unironic fright that puncture the comedy, reminding the player that the ghost is real and dangerous
promises.why: the Kernel asks for 'fright in equal measure'; without this, the story becomes a farce rather than a ghost story

set_pieces.scene: the mooring line snapping not by wind, but by the ghost's hand, leaving the boat drifting in a narrow channel while the brother-in-law screams at the price of the fuel

a midnight inspection where the ghost stands at the helm in full rigging, pointing out a 'defect' that is actually a crack in the hull only visible in the dark, while the brother-in-law tries to sleep in the cabin

the boat refusing to enter a lock because the ghost demands a 'proper salute' to the water, forcing the player to choose between performing a ridiculous ritual or finding a way to bypass the lock entirely

promises.tone_engine: Funny: the comedy arises from the mismatch between the ghost's archaic, serious nautical demeanor and the mundane financial anxiety of the brother-in-law, who tries to apply real-world logic to supernatural rules. Eerie: the fright is sustained by the boat's physical responsiveness to the ghost's mood; the timbers creak, the water level drops, and the shadows lengthen when the ghost is displeased, creating a constant low-level dread beneath the jokes.
obligatory_cast: the ghost's 'crew' of shadows or reflections that appear in the portholes, who mimic the player's movements with a slight, wrong delay
a canal towpath keeper or neighbor who sees the boat's strange movements and offers cryptic, helpful, or useless advice from the bank
must_not: no permanent death of the brother-in-law: the Kernel implies he is a companion to be managed, not a victim to be mourned, and his financial pressure must persist
no modern technology solving the ghost: the brief implies the solution is about 'labeling how to get the boat under way' through interaction with the ghost, not using a GPS or a tow truck
no romantic subplot with the ghost: the Kernel frames the relationship as one of authority and ownership, not affection

you stood at the helm and let Lake Kaur name the defect
